To aggrieve someone means to cause them to feel wronged, hurt, or treated unjustly. When you aggrieve someone, you don't just make them sad — you make them feel that something unfair has been done to them. The hurt comes specifically from a sense of injustice.

Think of it this way: if it rains on your wedding day, you feel sad. But if your wedding venue cancels on you at the last minute without reason — you feel aggrieved. The difference is that being aggrieved always carries a feeling of "this wasn't right, and I have reason to complain."
The Two Layers Inside the Word

"Aggrieve" carries two feelings packed into one:

  1. Emotional pain — a genuine sense of hurt or distress.
  2. A sense of injustice — the feeling that you were treated unfairly, denied something you deserved, or wronged in some way.

Both layers must be present. A person who is aggrieved is not simply unhappy — they are unhappy because they feel wronged.
How This Word Is Actually Used

Here is something very important to know: "aggrieve" in its plain verb form is quite rare in everyday speech. What you will encounter far more often is its past-tense / adjective form — "aggrieved" — and the common phrase "the aggrieved party."

In practice, you'll almost never hear someone say:

"The decision aggrieved him."

You will far more commonly hear:

"He felt aggrieved by the decision."
"She had an aggrieved expression on her face."
"The aggrieved employees filed a complaint."

So while "aggrieve" is the verb, most of its real-world power lives in the word "aggrieved" — used as an adjective to describe a person who has been wronged.
The Register: When Is This Word Used?

"Aggrieve" and "aggrieved" are formal words. You are most likely to encounter them in:

  • Legal and official contexts — "the aggrieved party" means the person who has suffered harm and has the right to seek justice or compensation.
  • Formal writing — journalism, literature, official reports.
  • Serious conversations — when someone wants to emphasize the weight of an injustice, not just a minor annoyance.

You would not typically use this word in casual conversation. A friend wouldn't say "I feel aggrieved that you ate my sandwich." They'd say "I'm annoyed" or "that wasn't cool." But a formal complaint letter or a courtroom? "Aggrieved" fits perfectly.

These examples go from simple to more nuanced, so you can see the word in action:

  • "The long delays and poor service aggrieved many passengers."

(The delays caused passengers to feel wronged and distressed.)

  • "She felt deeply aggrieved when her colleague received credit for her work."

(She felt hurt AND felt it was unjust — both layers are present.)

  • "Speaking in an aggrieved tone, he explained how the company had broken its promise."

(His voice carried both hurt and a sense of being wronged.)

  • "The court ruled in favor of the aggrieved party."

(Legal usage — the person who suffered an injustice.)

  • "The new rules aggrieved workers who had followed the old system for years."

(The change caused them distress and a feeling of unfair treatment.)

This is where many learners get confused, so let's clear it up:

Aggrieve vs. Upset/Hurt:
To upset or hurt someone is simply to cause them emotional pain — there's no implication of injustice. To aggrieve someone specifically means that pain comes from being wronged. All aggrieving upsets, but not all upsetting aggrieve.

Aggrieve vs. Offend:
To offend someone is to cause insult, often through words or actions that violate their values or feelings. To aggrieve is deeper and more serious — it suggests real harm or a real injustice, not just a feeling of insult.

Aggrieve vs. Anger:
You can be angered by something and not feel wronged by it (a loud noise might anger you). But to be aggrieved always involves a sense of injustice. Aggrieved people often are angry, but the anger comes from feeling they were treated unfairly.
The Full Picture in One Sentence

To aggrieve someone is to cause them pain that is rooted in injustice — to make them feel that they have been wronged, denied fairness, or treated badly in a way that gives them real reason to feel hurt and complain.

Whenever you see this word, whether as a verb or in its far more common form "aggrieved," ask yourself: Who was wronged, and by what unfair act? The answer to that question is always what "aggrieve" is pointing at.
